knowledge:
- key_parameters: mc.samples=Number of Monte Carlo Dirichlet instances; recommend 128+ for t-test, 1000 for rigorous effect size, and 16+ for ANOVA ;; denom=Method to select the denominator for log-ratio calculation (e.g., "all" for standard CLR, "iqlr" for inter-quartile log-ratio to handle up to 25% asymmetry, "user" for custom invariant features) ;; gamma=Scale uncertainty parameter; NULL ignores scale, 1e-3 represents minimal noise, 0.25 to 1 is recommended for most datasets, or can be a matrix of scale samples generated by `aldex.makeScaleMatrix` ;; paired.test=Boolean indicating whether to perform a paired test or repeated measures ;; CI=Boolean in `aldex.effect` to calculate 95% confidence intervals for the effect size
- alternatives: Point-estimate approaches (e.g., standard differential expression tools assuming Negative Binomial distributions) which are sensitive to sparsity and read depth and may fail to control FDR properly on compositional data ;; propr R package which integrates with `aldex.clr` output for proportionality analysis ;; aldex.kw for Kruskal-Wallis test (noted as slow and unsupported; `aldex.glm` is preferred instead)
- when_to_use: Differential abundance/expression analysis of high-throughput sequencing count data (RNA-Seq, meta-RNA-Seq, 16S rRNA, single-cell, SELEX) where data are compositional and scale/asymmetry uncertainty needs to be modeled
- pitfalls: Not accounting for scale or asymmetry can lead to high false positive rates (e.g., 80% FDR in asymmetric datasets when using standard CLR with `gamma = NULL`) ;; Using `aldex.kw` is extremely slow; users should use `aldex.glm` instead ;; Input data must not contain rows with all 0 values, as they will be removed by `aldex.clr` ;; Memory overflow can occur with very large datasets (thousands of samples, tens of thousands of features); the workaround is to run `aldex` with `mc.samples=2` multiple times and average the inference statistics

workflows.name: two_group_comparison
workflows.intent: Perform differential abundance testing between two groups using Welch's t-test, Wilcoxon rank test, and effect size estimation.
input: selex.sub (count matrix of features by samples)
workflows.stages: 1. Generate Dirichlet Monte Carlo instances using `aldex.clr` ;; 2. Perform t-tests using `aldex.ttest` ;; 3. Calculate effect sizes using `aldex.effect` ;; 4. Merge and plot results using `aldex.plot` and `aldex.plotFeature`
workflows.code:
data(selex)
#subset only the last 400 features for efficiency
selex.sub <- selex[1200:1600,]
conds <- c(rep("NS", 7), rep("S", 7))
x <- aldex.clr(selex.sub, conds, mc.samples=16, denom="all", verbose=F, gamma=1e-3)
x.tt <- aldex.ttest(x, hist.plot=F, paired.test=FALSE, verbose=FALSE,)
x.effect <- aldex.effect(x, CI=T, verbose=F, include.sample.summary=F,
  paired.test=FALSE, glm.conds=NULL, useMC=F)
x.all <- data.frame(x.tt,x.effect)
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
aldex.plot(x.all, type="MA", test="welch")
aldex.plot(x.all, type="MW", test="welch")
aldex.plotFeature(x, 'S:E:G:D')

workflows.name: complex_design_glm
workflows.intent: Perform differential abundance analysis for complex experimental designs with multiple covariates using GLMs.
input: selex.sub (count matrix of features by samples)
workflows.stages: 1. Generate CLR instances using model matrix in `aldex.clr` ;; 2. Fit GLM using `aldex.glm` ;; 3. Calculate GLM effect sizes using `aldex.glm.effect` ;; 4. Plot GLM results using `aldex.glm.plot`
workflows.code:
data(selex)
selex.sub <- selex[1200:1600, ]
covariates <- data.frame("A" = sample(0:1, 14, replace = TRUE),
   "B" = c(rep(0, 7), rep(1, 7)),
   "Z" = sample(c(1,2,3), 14, replace=TRUE))
mm <- model.matrix(~ A + Z + B, covariates)
x.glm <- aldex.clr(selex.sub, mm, mc.samples=4, denom="all", verbose=T)
glm.test <- aldex.glm(x.glm, mm, fdr.method='holm')
glm.eff<- aldex.glm.effect(x.glm)
aldex.glm.plot(glm.test, eff=glm.eff, contrast='B', type='MW', test='fdr')

workflows.name: scale_simulation
workflows.intent: Incorporate scale uncertainty or scale differences to correct for compositional asymmetry and control false positives.
input: selex.sub (count matrix of features by samples)
workflows.stages: 1. Create scale matrix using `aldex.makeScaleMatrix` ;; 2. Generate CLR instances with scale matrix in `aldex.clr` ;; 3. Calculate effect sizes and t-tests using `aldex.effect` and `aldex.ttest`
workflows.code:
set.seed(11)
data(selex)
selex.sub <- selex[1201:1600,]
conds <- c(rep("NS", 7), rep("S", 7))
# unscaled
x.u <- aldex.clr(selex.sub, conds, mc.samples=16, 
    gamma=1e-3, verbose=FALSE)
x.u.e <- aldex.effect(x.u, CI=T)

# scaled
# this represents and 8-fold difference in scale between groups
mu.mod <- c(rep(1,7), rep(8,7))
scale.model <- aldex.makeScaleMatrix(gamma=0.5, mu=mu.mod, conditions=conds, mc.samples=16, log=FALSE)
x.ss <- aldex.clr(selex.sub, conds, mc.samples=16, 
    gamma=scale.model, verbose=FALSE)
x.ss.e <- aldex.effect(x.ss, CI=T)
x.ss.tt <- aldex.ttest(x.ss)
x.ss.all <- cbind(x.ss.e, x.ss.tt)
aldex.plotFeature(x.u, 'S:D:S:D', pooledOnly=T)
aldex.plotFeature(x.ss, 'S:D:S:D', pooledOnly=T)

workflows.name: sensitivity_analysis
workflows.intent: Assess how differential abundance results change across a range of scale uncertainty (gamma) values.
input: Y (count matrix of features by samples)
workflows.stages: 1. Generate base CLR instances using `aldex.clr` ;; 2. Run sensitivity analysis using `aldex.senAnalysis` ;; 3. Plot sensitivity results using `plotGamma`
workflows.code:
gamma_to_test <- c(1e-3, .1, .25, .5, .75, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
##Run the CLR function
clr <- aldex.clr(Y, conds)
##Run sensitivity analysis function
sen_res <- aldex.senAnalysis(clr, gamma = gamma_to_test)
##Plotting
plotGamma(sen_res, thresh = .1)
